diagrams.title: Visible content loop
diagrams.caption: Browse, review the site map, open the rest by hand, repeat; a crawler helps but must exclude delete and admin links.
steps: Browse every link and finish multistage forms through a recording proxy.
Review the site map; the proxy parses every response.
Access the rest by hand, including what the spider found and you skipped.
Repeat.

when.fails: a client-routed page, or links inside dead compiled objects

diagrams.title: Spider then and now
diagrams.caption: An HTML-only spider sees a JavaScript app as empty; katana -jc parses its endpoints.

diagrams.title: Hidden content loop
diagrams.caption: Guess names, read code and size to tell a real hit from the custom 404, infer more names, add archived paths.
steps: Start from a wordlist.
Request each name with ffuf; -ac calibrates the fake-404 filter.
Read status code and size: a 200 can be a custom not-found page; 401 or 403 means closed but present.
Infer more names from what exists: AddDocument implies EditDocument; -e .bak,.old,.tmp.
Archives add paths: a path archived but 404 live is a route the app once served.

when.fails: one URL picks its function by parameter (section 3)

diagrams.title: Search operators
diagrams.caption: site:, quotes and - still work; link:, related: and cache: do not, and they fail silently.

diagrams.title: File tree or routing by value
diagrams.caption: A file tree yields to a wordlist; a URL that routes by parameter needs the schema, the API description, the JavaScript or parameter discovery.

when.applies: routing by value, not by path

diagrams.title: Entry points in a request
diagrams.caption: URL path, query, trusted headers, cookie and body all reach server logic; JSON keys are not verified.

diagrams.title: Out-of-band hit
diagrams.caption: The target resolves a name you control, so the OAST server logs a DNS hit though the page shows nothing.
steps: interactsh-client prints a name such as c23b2...oast.pro.
Send the name in a header: curl -s -H "X-Forwarded-For: c23b2...oast.pro" $TARGET.
The target resolves the name at the OAST server; the page shows nothing.
The client prints: Received DNS interaction (A).

diagrams.title: Fingerprint decision flow
diagrams.caption: Read the banner, extensions and error pages, cookie names; name the stack; look up each component in OSV.dev.
steps: Banner: curl -sI and httpx -sc -title -td; Server: Apache/1.3.31 names stack and version.
HTTP fingerprint: httprecon and httprint status not verified; httpx -td uses the Wappalyzer dataset.
Extensions and error pages: .asp .aspx .jsp .php .dll; curl -sI $TARGET/CookieAuth.dll.
Cookie and directory names: JSESSIONID, ASPSESSIONID, PHPSESSID, /servlet (not verified).
Name the stack: Apache-Coyote is Tomcat, a Java servlet container.
Find the third-party component and version, then research known flaws.
Query OSV.dev; an empty answer means no known entry, not no flaw.

when.applies: at least one signal is not stripped

diagrams.title: Reading request names
diagrams.caption: Names carry meaning: a flag to flip, an ORDER BY, and a REST path that maps to a hidden call whose action and id you can change.

when.applies: names read like a programmer and stay consistent

diagrams.title: Map, then plan, then attack
diagrams.caption: Build the content and functional maps, check core functions and third-party code, rank, and only then attack.
steps: Content map.
Functional map.
Know the core functions and mechanisms: session state, access control, authentication, recovery.
Match each feature to its usual bug class (not verified).
Check third-party code in OSV.dev and with nuclei -as.
Plan of attack: rank functions and bug classes; first probe all hosts with httpx.

when.fails: never: no tool maps an app safely alone
